title: Birds of the Woodland Edge
description: Meet familiar North American birds through direct clues about names, calls, and characteristic behavior.
cardDescription: Meet familiar North American birds through direct clues about names, calls, and characteristic behavior.
focus: Bird names can be more dependable than a color alone, since appearance changes with species, age, and sex. These clues use recognizable behavior or a clearly completed common name.
solvingTip: Try a completed bird name or a characteristic action first. Use the shorter bird words to help cross the longer names.

answerNotes.WOODPECKER: Woodpeckers use their bills for feeding and other activities. Their drilling behavior is a stronger clue than a single plumage color.
answerNotes.NUTHATCH: Nuthatches often work downward along bark. This behavior distinguishes the clue from a generic tree-climbing bird.
answerNotes.CHICKADEE: Chickadees are named for a recognizable call. Several North American species belong to this familiar group.
answerNotes.WAXWING: The red tips give waxwings their name. The tips are feather features rather than actual drops of wax.
answerNotes.TOWHEE: Towhees are sparrows often seen scratching in leaf litter. The pronunciation cue supports an otherwise less familiar spelling.

title: Mammals by the Creek
description: Explore the words for streamside mammals, their homes, and the movements they make in and around the water.
cardDescription: Explore the words for streamside mammals, their homes, and the movements they make in and around the water.
focus: These clues distinguish animals from the structures they occupy. A beaver may build a dam and a lodge, while several other mammals also live along stream banks without building either one.
solvingTip: A home, a barrier, and an animal are different kinds of answers. Let the definition’s category guide your first letters.

To move through water using the body and limbs
To plunge beneath the water's surface
Sheltered resting or breeding place of a wild mammal
Foot impression left by a creekside animal

answerNotes.BEAVER: Beavers can modify waterways with dams, but not every beaver colony builds one. The broad flattened tail is another useful feature.
answerNotes.OTTER: An otter is a mammal adapted to aquatic life. It differs from a beaver in both body shape and its usual feeding habits.
answerNotes.MUSKRAT: A muskrat is a rodent, as a beaver is. Its tail is narrow rather than broad and paddle-shaped.
answerNotes.LODGE: A lodge is a dwelling. A dam is a barrier that holds water back, so the two structures have different functions.
answerNotes.DAM: A dam can raise the water level. It is not the same structure as the lodge in which a beaver family lives.

title: Frogs and Their Neighbors
description: Learn the names and body features of amphibians often associated with damp places and freshwater.
cardDescription: Learn the names and body features of amphibians often associated with damp places and freshwater.
focus: Typical frog development provides a familiar example, but amphibian life cycles are diverse. The clues use qualified descriptions rather than assuming every member of the group develops in the same way.
solvingTip: Decide whether a clue describes the whole animal, an early life stage, or a body part. Watch the distinction between a broad group and one member.

answerNotes.AMPHIBIAN: Amphibians include several distinct groups. Many have aquatic young, but their life cycles have important exceptions.
answerNotes.TOAD: Toads are within the broader frog group. The familiar distinction is not a division into two unrelated animal groups.
answerNotes.SALAMANDER: Salamanders usually keep a tail as adults. Adult frogs typically do not.
answerNotes.GILLS: Many tadpoles use gills. Some salamanders retain gills as adults, so the feature does not belong only to young animals.
answerNotes.SKIN: Amphibian skin can play a role in gas exchange. This is different from saying that all their breathing occurs through the skin.

answerNotes.TURTLE: Different turtles live in different habitats; this scene features a pond visitor.
answerNotes.SHELL: The shell includes a top and underside; no technical part names are needed here.
answerNotes.TAIL: A turtle's tail is separate from its legs.
answerNotes.NECK: Some turtles can pull their head and neck back toward the shell.
answerNotes.LOG: A log can provide a resting place above the water.

title: Fish in a River
description: Identify familiar freshwater fish and the parts and movements associated with life in flowing water.
cardDescription: Identify familiar freshwater fish and the parts and movements associated with life in flowing water.
focus: Fish differ in body coverings and feeding features. The clues avoid treating every species alike and distinguish an animal’s name from the water feature or body part around it.
solvingTip: Use the distinctive feature or completed common name for a fish. Short body-part words can supply crossings for the longer names.

answerNotes.CATFISH: Those feelers are barbels rather than mammalian whisker hairs. They help explain the familiar name.
answerNotes.TROUT: Rainbow trout is a familiar species name. The completed name is more specific than a general description of a spotted fish.
answerNotes.PIKE: Pike are predatory fish. Their elongated body and snout distinguish this clue from other common freshwater names.
answerNotes.GILL: A gill obtains oxygen dissolved in water. Fish are not separating oxygen from the chemical structure of water molecules.
answerNotes.SCALE: Many fish have scales, but some do not have the familiar overlapping covering. Catfish are one reason not to generalize to every fish.
